strengths: Slides 2–7 form a manager-relevant argument from guest need through ritual, operating model, economics, and pilot.
Slide 3 makes the proposed hour concrete with a clearly timed five-stage sequence.
Slide 6 explicitly labels the financial model as illustrative and shows enough arithmetic to audit the $3,500 base case.
Slides 1, 3, and 8 use hospitality imagery that gives the offer a calm, property-based setting.

issues.evidence: [Generation defect] White text inside the two pale-teal proposition cards has very weak contrast, especially the smaller descriptions.
issues.fix: Use dark-teal text on the pale cards or darken the cards substantially; verify projection contrast for the body copy.

issues.evidence: [Selection defect] The image focuses on a hand placing a key beside towels and water, which reads more as check-in or housekeeping than as the restorative ritual being sold.
issues.fix: Use an image showing the hosted guest experience, practitioner interaction, or prepared ritual setting.

issues.evidence: [Generation defect] The bottom disclaimer is visibly crowded into the frame edge, wraps awkwardly, and collides with the page number, leaving the final line partially clipped.
issues.fix: Raise and reflow the disclaimer as a single readable footer and move the page number to an independent margin position.

issues.evidence: Five narrow text columns make the operational explanations noticeably smaller and denser than surrounding slides.
issues.fix: Convert the sequence into a two-level service blueprint or split it across two slides so responsibilities and handoffs can be scanned.

issues.evidence: The exclusions and 30-day assumption are rendered as very small, pale footer text even though they materially qualify the economics.
issues.fix: Increase the caveat size and contrast and place key exclusions beside the contribution result.

issues.evidence: [Generation defect] The lower-left 'End of week 6' stage and the bottom of the decision-gate table run beyond the slide boundary. The pilot's conclusion and part of its success criteria cannot be read.
issues.fix: Rebuild the slide on a horizontal six-week timeline, shorten the phase descriptions, and keep every gate within a tested safe area.

A.signatureMoment: Slide 6 is the strongest substantive moment: an auditable illustrative formula and fill-sensitivity chart translate the wellness idea into a manager decision.

strengths: Slide 1 is a memorable editorial opening with a clear promise, a room configured for the ritual, and an immediate guest-versus-manager value split.
Slide 3 turns the hour into a highly scannable sequence and uses the highlighted Restore stage to establish the experiential peak.
Slide 5 clearly separates the boutique-hospitality proposition from its backstage operating requirements.
Slide 6 presents the base-case contribution, cost bridge, sensitivity, and break-even assumption in one manager-friendly view.
Slide 8 closes with three specific decisions rather than a generic sales call to action.
The restrained typography, rules, numbering, and warm green system remain coherent from opening through close.

issues.evidence: The three category icons are so pale that they nearly disappear against the ivory background and contribute little to comprehension.
issues.fix: Increase icon contrast or replace them with more informative guest, staff, and property signals.

issues.evidence: [Generation defect] The third large operating assumption is cut off at the bottom; only the top of 'Minute room turn after each session' is visible.
issues.fix: Reduce or reposition the left-column metrics so the full 15-minute room-turn assumption fits inside the slide.

issues.evidence: The 35% fill case appears only as an almost invisible line near zero, so the slightly negative outcome is not explicit.
issues.fix: Label that bar approximately −$0.1k and use a distinct negative treatment below the baseline.

issues.evidence: [Generation defect] The lower row of decision-gate cards is visibly cut by the bottom edge, obscuring supporting labels and making the complete gate set unavailable.
issues.fix: Compress the upper timeline or reduce the gate cards to a single six-item row with all labels inside the safe area.

issues.evidence: The narrow top photograph is atmospheric but shows only a wall, water, and shadows; it does not reinforce the proposed hosted experience or decision.
issues.fix: Use a closing image of the prepared room or guest handoff that visually completes the story introduced on slide 1.

B.signatureMoment: Slide 6 pairs a legible fill-sensitivity chart with a large $3,500 base-case card and transparent cost arithmetic, giving managers a usable commercial discussion tool.

result.reason: B is the deck I would give this user after correcting its two clipping defects. It has the stronger hospitality editorial system, cleaner information hierarchy, and more purposeful pacing; its operating, financial, and pilot slides are easier for managers to scan. Neither rendered deck is currently ready because both fail the unclipped-content hard check. A's additional photographic and layout complexity does not earn its keep: its low-contrast opening cards and severely broken slide 7 outweigh the extra imagery. The single most valuable improvement to A would be a complete presentation-safe re-typesetting pass beginning with slide 7 and the slide 1 contrast failure. B exceeds competent default quality through tailored commercial clarity, but not by enough to qualify as exceptional.
result.whatWouldMakeWinnerExceptional: First eliminate the slide 5 and 7 clipping, then replace one of the conventional box-and-timeline compositions with a genuinely integrated service blueprint showing the guest experience above the line and staff roles, room reset, evidence, and economics below it in one property-customizable visual.
